content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) developed a revised classification system for HIV infection in children in 1994, replacing the previous pediatric HIV classification system established in 1987. This updated system was created in response to advancements in understanding the progression of HIV disease in children. For the purposes of the CDC classification, a child is defined as an individual under 13 years of age. Standard anti-HIV IgG antibody tests are not reliable for determining a child’s HIV infection status before 18 months of age due to the presence of maternal antibodies. Therefore, viral antigen tests are utilized for diagnosis in this age group. In the revised classification system, children infected with HIV are categorized into mutually exclusive groups based on three parameters. This system is designed to reflect the stage of the child’s disease, ensure clear and distinct classification categories, and balance simplicity with medical accuracy. Additionally, the document outlines updated pediatric definitions for two AIDS-defining conditions. Diagnosing HIV infection in infants born to HIV-infected mothers is complicated by the presence of maternal anti-HIV IgG antibodies, which cross the placenta to the fetus. As a result, nearly all infants born to HIV-infected mothers test positive for HIV antibodies at birth, even though only 15% to 30% of these infants are actually infected with the virus. Category N: Not Symptomatic Children in this category exhibit no signs or symptoms attributable to HIV infection. Alternatively, they may have only one of the conditions listed under Category A. Category A: Mildly Symptomatic Children in this category present with two or more of the following conditions but do not exhibit any of the conditions listed under Categories B or C: Lymphadenopathy (enlarged lymph nodes greater than 0.5 cm at more than two sites; bilateral involvement counts as one site) Hepatomegaly (enlarged liver) Splenomegaly (enlarged spleen) Dermatitis Parotitis (inflammation of the parotid gland) Recurrent or persistent upper respiratory infections, sinusitis, or otitis media (middle ear infections) Category B: Moderately Symptomatic Children in this category have symptomatic conditions that are attributed to HIV infection but are not included in the definitions for Categories A or C.
